summary.text: Cosmology is the study of the nature of the universe, the cosmos.
Physical cosmology is the branch of astronomy that treats the universe as a whole, including its origin, its large-scale structure and its ultimate fate.
Because light travels at a finite speed, looking out into space is looking back in time, which led one astrophysicist to call cosmology a historical science.

items.prompt: An astronomer says every photo of a faraway galaxy is a picture of the past. What makes that true?

options.label: Telescope lenses bend incoming light, which delays each image a lot
Galaxies change so fast that only old images can ever be captured
Light moves at a limited speed, so what we see left the galaxy long ago
Cameras need such long exposures that the picture is years out of date

items.explain: Light takes time to cross space, so looking far away means looking back in time.

items.prompt: A rock drops in a field and a planet circles the Sun. What did Newton's cosmology assume about the rules behind both?

options.label: Both obey the same physical laws
Each follows its own rules, set by where it sits
Only the planet follows laws, since it moves forever
Earth's laws apply only to things below the Moon

items.explain: The Copernican principle, a basis of Newton's cosmology, says bodies on Earth obey the same laws as all celestial bodies.

items.prompt: In 1920 astronomers argued over whether spiral nebulae were separate star systems. What settled the question?

options.label: Distances to Cepheid stars in Andromeda placed it beyond the Milky Way
A vote at the 1920 meeting favored the larger universe
Einstein's equations showed no other galaxies could exist
Telescopes showed the nebulae were gas clouds inside the Milky Way

items.explain: Hubble detected Cepheid variables in the Andromeda Galaxy in 1923 and 1924, and their distance put spiral nebulae well beyond the Milky Way.

items.prompt: After Hubble's redshift work, which later find strengthened Lemaître's Big Bang proposal?

options.label: A new planet orbiting the Sun in a way Newton predicted
The cosmic microwave background, found by Penzias and Wilson
Proof that the Milky Way is the only star system
The discovery that the Earth sits at the cosmic center

items.explain: The Big Bang model was corroborated by Hubble's redshift discovery and later by the discovery of the cosmic microwave background by Penzias and Wilson.

items.prompt: In the 1800s puzzles like why the night sky is dark clashed with Newtonian gravity. What did they together point to?

options.label: A universe that is not infinite
A universe that is infinitely old and unchanging
A universe with no stars beyond the Milky Way
A universe where gravity fades out at long range

items.explain: Olbers' paradox and the two others all indicated a non-infinite universe.

items.prompt: Around 1990 cosmology shifted from a largely speculative science to a predictive one. What drove the change?

options.label: Philosophers agreeing on the meaning of the cosmos
New laws of motion replacing Newton's
Satellite and survey observations that matched theory precisely
A ban on theories that cannot be tested

items.explain: Advances such as the COBE, WMAP and Planck satellites and large redshift surveys brought precise agreement between theory and observation.

paragraphs.heading: What cosmology is
paragraphs.text: Cosmology is the study of the universe, the cosmos, and of what it is fundamentally like. Its name joins Greek words for the universe or the world and for study. Scientists such as astronomers and physicists work on it, and so do philosophers, including those who think about physics, space and time. Because it shares ground with philosophy, a cosmological theory can mix scientific and non-scientific claims and can rest on assumptions that no one is able to test. Religious or mythological cosmology is something else: beliefs drawn from creation myths and traditions about the end of things.

paragraphs.heading: Physical cosmology
paragraphs.text: Inside astronomy, physical cosmology is the branch concerned with the universe as a whole. It asks how the universe began, how its history unfolded, how its largest structures are arranged and move, and how it will finally end, along with the physical laws behind all of that. The leading theory today is the Big Bang, in a standard version called the Lambda-CDM model that includes dark matter and dark energy. On this picture, the Big Bang was followed almost at once by cosmic inflation, a stretching of space out of which the universe is believed to have emerged. That happened 13.799 ± 0.021 billion years ago.

paragraphs.heading: From Ptolemy to Newton
paragraphs.text: In its earliest form, cosmology was what is now called celestial mechanics, the study of the heavens. Greek thinkers such as Aristarchus of Samos, Aristotle and Ptolemy put forward different theories. Ptolemy's Earth-centred system held sway until the 16th century, when Nicolaus Copernicus, and after him Johannes Kepler and Galileo Galilei, proposed a Sun-centred one. In 1687 Isaac Newton's Principia Mathematica gave the first description of the law of universal gravitation. It supplied a physical reason for Kepler's laws and cleared up oddities in older systems that came from the planets pulling on one another. Newton's cosmology also held that things on Earth obey the same physical laws as bodies in the sky, an idea known as the Copernican principle.

paragraphs.heading: Einstein and an expanding universe
paragraphs.text: Modern scientific cosmology is widely dated to 1917, when Albert Einstein published a paper titled Cosmological Considerations of the General Theory of Relativity. Physicists then began dropping the assumption of a static, unchanging universe. In 1922 Alexander Friedmann put forward an expanding universe with matter in motion. Later models explored whether the cosmological constant from Einstein's 1917 paper might produce an expanding universe, depending on its value. In 1927 the Belgian priest Georges Lemaître proposed the Big Bang model, which was later backed by Edwin Hubble's discovery of redshift in 1929 and by the 1964 discovery of the cosmic microwave background by Arno Penzias and Robert Woodrow Wilson.

paragraphs.heading: The Great Debate
paragraphs.text: Heber Curtis held that the spiral nebulae seen in telescopes were star systems in their own right, island universes, while Harlow Shapley of Mount Wilson argued that the cosmos was made up of the Milky Way alone. The clash peaked at the Great Debate, held on 26 April 1920 at a meeting of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States in Washington. Edwin Hubble settled it in 1923 and 1924 by finding Cepheid variables in the Andromeda Galaxy. Their distance put spiral nebulae well outside the edge of the Milky Way.

paragraphs.heading: Puzzles of Newtonian gravity
paragraphs.text: In the 19th century, Newton's gravity ran into several paradoxes: why the sky is dark (Olbers' paradox), why gravity does not pull the universe into collapse (the Bentley–Seeliger paradox), and why the universe has not reached thermal equilibrium (the heat death paradox). All three pointed toward a universe that is not infinite.

paragraphs.heading: A predictive science
paragraphs.text: Since about 1990, major leaps in observation have turned cosmology from a mostly speculative field into a predictive one, where theory and measurement agree closely. Among them are readings of the microwave background taken by the COBE, WMAP and Planck satellites, big new galaxy redshift surveys such as 2dfGRS and SDSS, and studies of distant supernovae and gravitational lensing.
